summary: Specifies tunneling over MAPOS networks, allowing a MAPOS network to give a transparent point-to-point link for PPP over SONET/SDH without extra overhead.

eli5.summary: It lets one kind of network pretend to be a plain wire for another.

questions: why would you use mapos ppp tunneling
subtitle: Tunneling PPP over SONET/SDH through MAPOS networks

tldr.problem: Organizations may want to connect PPP equipment across a MAPOS network, but the network and the equipment use slightly different frame formats, creating overhead and complexity.
tldr.mechanism: MAPOS/PPP tunneling mode uses header rewriting: MAPOS switches rewrite frame headers at entry and exit points to make the network transparent to the PPP equipment, allowing a MAPOS network to provide a point-to-point link with no additional overhead.
tldr.outcome: This enables efficient L2 multiplexing where multiple PPP connections can share the cost of high-speed SONET/SDH links through a MAPOS network, with near-zero overhead.

today: RFC 3186 is an Informational document describing MAPOS/PPP tunneling as one implementation approach in the broader MAPOS ecosystem. MAPOS itself has seen limited widespread deployment compared to other optical transport technologies like MPLS. However, the tunneling mode remains a valid approach for multiplexing multiple point-to-point connections over optical networks when MAPOS infrastructure is in use. The concept of using header rewriting for transparent tunneling has influenced later technologies.

sections.title: What MAPOS/PPP Tunneling Does
sections.content:
MAPOS (Multiple Access Protocol over SONET/SDH) is a protocol for carrying multiple data streams over SONET/SDH optical links. PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) over SONET/SDH is a standard way to run a single data connection over SONET/SDH. The two protocols use very similar frame formats: MAPOS v1 and PPP both have an 8-bit address field and an 8-bit control field followed by a 16-bit protocol field. MAPOS 16 has a 16-bit address field.

MAPOS/PPP tunneling mode exploits this similarity: by rewriting just one or two octets at the network edge, a MAPOS network can provide a transparent point-to-point link for PPP-based equipment. This avoids the overhead of encapsulation and allows multiple PPP connections to share one MAPOS network, reducing the cost of high-speed long-haul links for customers.
sections.eli5: MAPOS and PPP frames look almost the same. By rewriting a couple of bytes at the edges, a MAPOS network can act like a simple link between two PPP devices.

sections.title: How Header Rewriting Works
sections.content:
In MAPOS/PPP tunneling mode, PPP customer equipment (CPE) connects to border MAPOS switches. At the ingress switch, when a frame arrives from CPE with PPP headers (0xFF and 0x03 as address and control fields), these octets are rewritten to a MAPOS destination address (such as 0x0403 for a specific peer CPE). The frame is then forwarded through the MAPOS network.

Inside the border switch, several steps occur: SONET/SDH framing is processed, HDLC byte-stuffing is reversed, FCS (frame check sequence) is verified and discarded, the address/control bytes are rewritten, a new MAPOS-FCS is calculated, and the frame is re-framed for SONET/SDH transmission. At the egress switch, the reverse happens: the MAPOS address is rewritten back to 0xFF03, and the frame is returned to standard PPP format.

Because the PPP equipment never sees the MAPOS network, it experiences the MAPOS network as a transparent point-to-point link. The rewriting happens entirely at the border switches and requires no configuration at the CPE side.
sections.eli5: The ingress switch replaces the PPP address label with a MAPOS address, routers forward the frame inside the MAPOS network, and the egress switch restores the PPP label.

sections.title: Setup and Management
sections.content:
To establish a MAPOS/PPP tunneling path, operators choose a pair of MAPOS addresses (one on the ingress switch and one on the egress switch) and configure those ports to PPP tunneling mode. This disables NSP (Node Switch Protocol) and SSP (Switch-Switch Protocol), disables multicast forwarding, enables header rewriting, and sets the correct SONET/SDH path signal label (C2 byte).

When configured properly and after routes stabilize, the PPP link can come up and data flows normally. PPP keep-alive (LCP Echo) is used for end-to-end link detection; if either side of the path fails, the keep-alive will timeout and the CPE will mark the link down. Within the MAPOS cloud, SSP handles topology changes and provides restoration within seconds.

A path database tracks which MAPOS address-pairs correspond to which customer links, useful for operational management but not used for frame forwarding. Operators must carefully avoid misconfiguration such as path duplication. Configuration can be reversed by disabling the port's PPP tunneling mode, which re-enables NSP, SSP, and multicast forwarding.
sections.eli5: Operators configure which ports should do header rewriting and which MAPOS address to rewrite to. PPP equipment pings across the link regularly to notice if the path fails.

sections.title: Performance and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Because MAPOS lacks QoS control and PPP has no flow-control feature, guaranteeing end-to-end throughput is difficult. Operators should provision sufficient bandwidth on inter-switch links to support all paths they place on those links. Switches are recommended to ensure per-port fairness using appropriate queuing, which is especially important for over-subscribed configurations.

The RFC recommends using MAPOS 16 instead of MAPOS v1 for easier address management, since each port corresponds to one MAPOS address. Automatic address negotiation is not suitable for PPP tunneling mode because path management becomes complex.

The latency evaluation shows that the header rewriting introduces minimal delay compared to basic SONET/SDH transmission or L3 routing, making it practical for delay-sensitive applications. The RFC notes that optical protection (with sub-50ms restoration) and backup links can provide redundancy, sharing the cost across multiple tunneled paths.
sections.eli5: You need enough bandwidth on the network links between switches to handle all the tunneled connections. The overhead is very small, so latency stays low.
